The Night Sky: Constellations and Coordinates
Your first map of the universe

Before telescopes, the sky was the only map, clock and calendar humans had. Farmers planted by it. Sailors steered by it. Look up on a clear night far from city lights and you can see roughly 2,500 stars at a time. They look like dots on a dome. They are not. They sit at wildly different distances. This lesson gives you the language for finding your way around that dome.
Constellations are patterns, not families

A constellation is a pattern we imagine by joining bright stars. The stars in it are usually unrelated. One may be 40 light-years away, its neighbour 800. Every culture drew its own pictures. In 1922-1930 the International Astronomical Union fixed 88 official constellations , each a patch of sky with firm borders, like countries on a map. Orion, Ursa Major (the Great Bear, with the Saptarishi 'Big Dipper') and Crux (the Southern Cross) are familiar ones.
The celestial sphere

Imagine all stars painted on a huge sphere around Earth. It is a useful fiction: we cannot feel depth in the sky, but we can measure directions exactly. Extend Earth's axis outward and you get the north celestial pole . Extend the equator and you get the celestial equator . The whole sphere seems to turn once a day, but that is really Earth spinning the other way: 15 degrees every hour.
Why the Pole Star stays put

Polaris lies within about 1 degree of the north celestial pole, so as Earth spins it hardly moves. Everything else circles it. In India it is Dhruva. A neat trick: the height of Polaris above your horizon equals your latitude . At Delhi (28.6 N) it sits about 28 degrees up. At the equator it sits on the horizon. At the North Pole it is straight overhead. Navigators used this for centuries.
Two ways to give a star an address

Horizon system: altitude (angle above horizon) and azimuth (compass direction). Easy, but it changes with place and time. Equatorial system: fixed to the stars, like latitude and longitude. Declination is the north-south angle from the celestial equator. Right ascension is the east-west position, measured in hours (0 to 24) from the point where the Sun crosses the equator at the March equinox. Because the address is fixed to the stars, a star keeps the same coordinates wherever you stand.
The sky changes with the hour and the season

Through one night stars rise in the east and set in the west. Through the year, the same star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night, because Earth moves along its orbit. After a year the pattern returns. This is why Orion rules winter evenings and Scorpius rules summer ones: in different seasons our night side faces different parts of space. Also, the pole slowly wobbles like a spinning top, called precession , taking about 26,000 years. Around 3000 BCE the pole star was Thuban; in about 12,000 years it will be Vega.
Measuring the invisible

Positions were first measured with sighting rods, quadrants and later the telescope. Hipparchus (c. 130 BCE) made a star catalogue and noticed precession by comparing his data with older records. He also began the magnitude scale for brightness. Today the ESA's Gaia satellite (launched 2013) has measured the positions of nearly two billion stars to a tiny fraction of a milli-arcsecond. Old records, new satellites: same method, sharper tools.
Three common mistakes

'Stars in a constellation are close.' No. They only line up from our viewpoint. 'The Pole Star is the brightest star.' No. Polaris is only moderately bright. Sirius is the brightest in the night sky. 'Astrology and astronomy are linked science.' The zodiac constellations are real star patterns, but no experiment has shown that star positions shape human lives.
Nakshatras, Saptarishi and Jantar Mantar

Indian astronomers divided the Moon's path into 27 nakshatras (lunar mansions): about one for each night the Moon takes to cross the sky. They appear in the Vedic texts and are still used in the panchang. The Saptarishi are the seven bright stars of Ursa Major. Their two end stars point toward Dhruva. Mriga (Orion) and Lubdhaka (Sirius) are named in Indian lore. Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built the stone observatories called Jantar Mantar (Delhi 1724, Jaipur and others) to measure star and Sun positions with huge masonry instruments.
Key takeaways

Constellations are 88 official sky regions; their stars are not physically linked. The celestial sphere is a model: poles and equator are Earth's extended outward. Polaris' altitude equals your latitude. Right ascension and declination fix a star's address. Precession shifts the pole star over about 26,000 years. Think about it: (1) Why would an observer in Chennai see stars that a person in Srinagar never sees? (2) If the Sun were removed, would the constellations visibly change within your lifetime? Why?
Motions of Sun, Moon and Planets
The sky is a clock with moving hands

Stars keep their pattern night after night. Five bright 'stars' do not: they drift across the pattern. The Greeks called them planetes , wanderers. With the Sun and Moon, they were the seven moving bodies behind our week. Understanding their motion was the puzzle that led, step by step, to modern physics.
The Sun's yearly path

Against the stars, the Sun appears to travel along a great circle called the ecliptic , once a year, about 1 degree a day. The zodiac constellations lie along this line. The ecliptic is tilted 23.4 degrees to the celestial equator. That tilt is why the Sun climbs high in summer and low in winter, and why the Sun's rising point shifts north and south through the year.
Phases of the Moon

The Moon shines by reflected sunlight. Half of it is always lit. What changes is how much of the lit half we see, as the Moon orbits Earth. New Moon: Moon between us and the Sun, the lit side faces away. Full Moon: Earth between, the lit side faces us. Cycle length from one new Moon to the next: 29.5 days (synodic month). The Moon orbits Earth in 27.3 days against the stars, but Earth moves on around the Sun meanwhile, so it needs about two extra days to line up again with the Sun.
Planets: wandering lights

Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are easy to see without a telescope. Planets do not twinkle much, because they show tiny discs rather than points. Mercury and Venus orbit inside Earth's path, so they never stray far from the Sun: you see them just after sunset or before sunrise. Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can appear anywhere along the ecliptic, even at midnight.
Retrograde loops: Earth overtaking

Mars normally drifts eastward among the stars. Every 26 months or so it stops, moves backward for weeks, then resumes. This is retrograde motion . Nothing reverses. Earth, on the inner and faster track, overtakes Mars, like passing a slower car on the highway: the car seems to slide backward against distant trees. This one fact was the strongest clue for a Sun-centred system.
Orbits obey simple rules

Planets orbit in nearly the same plane, which is why they all follow the ecliptic. Closer planets move faster: Mercury circles the Sun in 88 days, Earth in 365.25, Jupiter in 11.86 years, Saturn in 29.5 years. Each planet's year grows quickly with distance. Kepler later captured this in an exact law (lesson 4).
Watching patiently

Babylonian priests recorded planets for centuries. Greek, Indian and Islamic astronomers refined predictions. Retrograde loops were traced night by night on charts. A modern amateur can repeat it: mark Mars against the stars once a week for six months and the loop appears. Today radar and spacecraft ranging give distances to planets within metres.
Clearing it up

'The Moon makes its own light.' No, reflected sunlight. 'Phases are Earth's shadow.' No. Earth's shadow causes lunar eclipses, which are rare. Phases are just viewing angle. 'Retrograde planets influence our lives.' The reversal is a viewing illusion, not a physical event.
Graha, tithi and Aryabhata

Indian astronomy tracked Surya, Chandra and five planets (grahas), with Rahu and Ketu as the two lunar nodes. The Hindu tithi is one thirtieth of the lunar month, based on Moon-Sun angle. Aryabhata (born 476 CE, Aryabhatiya, 499 CE) proposed that Earth rotates, so the stars only seem to circle us. Brahmagupta (628 CE) and Bhaskara II (1150 CE) gave calculation methods for planetary positions still used for the panchang.
Key takeaways

Sun, Moon and five planets move against the fixed stars along the ecliptic. Moon phases are viewing geometry; the cycle is 29.5 days. Retrograde motion is Earth overtaking an outer planet. Inner planets stay near the Sun; outer ones roam the whole ecliptic. Think about it: (1) Why can Venus never be seen at midnight? (2) If retrograde were real motion of Mars, what else would we see?
Eclipses, Seasons and Calendars
The sky that frightened and taught us

A total solar eclipse turns day into dusk in minutes. People once feared it. Today it is one of the best demonstrations of how orderly the sky really is: we can predict eclipses centuries ahead. The same geometry of tilt and orbit explains seasons and shapes every calendar.
Solar eclipse: the Moon blocks the Sun

At new Moon, the Moon can pass exactly between Earth and Sun. Its shadow falls on a narrow strip of Earth. Inside the dark centre ( umbra ) you see a total eclipse; in the lighter outer shadow ( penumbra ) a partial one. The coincidence is remarkable: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther, so they look almost the same size in the sky.
Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow on the Moon

At full Moon, Earth may sit between the Sun and Moon, so the Moon passes into Earth's shadow. The Moon turns coppery red, because the only light reaching it has bent through Earth's atmosphere, with blue scattered away (the same reason sunsets are red). A lunar eclipse is visible from the whole night side of Earth. A total solar eclipse is visible only along a thin path.
Why not every month?

If the Moon orbited in the same plane as Earth's orbit, we would get an eclipse every month. But the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees . Most months the Moon passes above or below the line. Eclipses occur only near the two points where the orbits cross, the nodes . The pattern repeats every saros , about 18 years 11 days 8 hours, a cycle known to the Babylonians.
Seasons: tilt, not distance

Earth's axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees. When the northern half leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits at a steeper angle and days are longer: summer. Six months later it is winter there. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in northern winter. So distance cannot be the cause.
Calendars: matching Sun and Moon

The year (365.2422 days) and the lunar month (29.53 days) do not fit evenly: 12 lunar months is only 354 days. Cultures chose: purely solar (Gregorian), purely lunar (Islamic), or lunisolar with a leap month (Hindu, Chinese, Jewish). The Gregorian calendar, adopted from 1582, drops three leap days in every 400 years (century years are leap only if divisible by 400) to stay in step with the seasons.
Prediction is the proof

In 1919, an eclipse let Eddington test Einstein's idea that gravity bends starlight. Eclipses also revealed the Sun's corona and, in 1868, a new element: helium (lesson 5). Computing eclipses backward matches historical records of eclipses in Babylon and China, which confirms that Earth's rotation is slowing slightly (about 2 milliseconds per century).
Watch out

'Summer is when Earth is nearest the Sun.' False; January is nearest. 'An eclipse is dangerous in itself.' The danger is looking at the Sun without proper eclipse glasses, which can burn the retina. 'Eclipses are omens.' They are geometry.
Aryabhata, Saka calendar, Kurukshetra

Aryabhata (499 CE) explained eclipses correctly as shadows of Earth and Moon, rather than the demon Rahu swallowing the Sun, and gave a method to compute them. India's national civil calendar is the Saka calendar (adopted 1957, year starting 22 March in ordinary years). It came from the 1952 Calendar Reform Committee chaired by the astrophysicist Meghnad Saha . Many Indian festivals still follow lunisolar rules in the panchang. India saw a total solar eclipse on 24 October 1995 and an annular one on 26 December 2019 in the south.
Key takeaways

Solar eclipse: new Moon blocks the Sun; lunar eclipse: full Moon enters Earth's shadow. The Moon's 5 degree tilt makes eclipses rare; the saros repeats them. Seasons come from the 23.4 degree tilt, not distance. Calendars reconcile year and month: solar, lunar or lunisolar. Think about it: (1) Why can a lunar eclipse be seen by many more people than a solar one? (2) What would seasons be like if Earth had no tilt?
From Ptolemy to Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo
How a hard-headed puzzle became a revolution

For 1,400 years Earth was the centre of the universe. Then, in 150 years, we learned it was just a planet. This is the story of how science changes its mind: not by opinion but by better measurement and sharper reasoning.
Ptolemy: a model that predicts

Claudius Ptolemy (c. 150 CE, Almagest ) put Earth at the centre. To explain retrograde loops he had planets move on small circles ( epicycles ) whose centres move on larger circles ( deferents ). The model worked for predictions and lasted over a millennium. It is not stupid: it matched observations. Its weakness was growing complexity.
Copernicus: the simpler arrangement

Nicolaus Copernicus , in De revolutionibus (1543), put the Sun at the centre and set Earth moving. Retrograde motion became a natural effect of Earth overtaking planets, without big epicycles. Earth now had three motions: rotating daily, orbiting yearly and a slow tilt shift. An early heliocentric idea had been made by Aristarchus of Samos around 270 BCE, but it did not win.
Tycho: better data

Tycho Brahe (1546-1601) built large instruments and recorded planetary positions for decades, to about 1 arcminute precision, the best before the telescope. He did not accept Earth's motion, but his data decided the matter later.
Kepler's three laws

Johannes Kepler used Tycho's Mars data to find that orbits are not circles: Ellipse law (1609): planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. Equal-area law (1609): a line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so planets move faster when closer. Harmonic law (1619): T squared is proportional to a cubed (period vs average distance).
Galileo: the telescope as evidence

In 1610 Galileo ( Sidereus Nuncius ) saw four moons orbiting Jupiter, so not everything orbits Earth. He saw the full set of phases of Venus, which only fit if Venus circles the Sun. He saw lunar mountains, sunspots and countless new stars in the Milky Way. In 1633 the Inquisition forced him to recant. The evidence stayed.
Newton: the why

Kepler described how planets move; Isaac Newton explained why. In the Principia (1687) he showed that one law of gravity (force falls as the square of distance) produces Kepler's three laws and also explains falling apples and tides. Gravity on Earth and in the sky was suddenly one thing.
The test that settled it

Predictions had to match nature. Venus's phases favoured the Sun-centred view; Tycho's precise data forced ellipses; stellar parallax, a tiny yearly shift in star positions, finally proved Earth's motion when Friedrich Bessel measured it for the star 61 Cygni in 1838. Models are kept when they predict, dropped when they cannot.
Common myths

'Everyone before Columbus thought Earth was flat.' Educated people knew it was round; Eratosthenes estimated its size about 240 BCE. 'Copernicus's circles were exact.' His system still used small epicycles; Kepler's ellipses fixed it. 'Galileo invented the telescope.' The Dutch did, in 1608; he improved it and pointed it at the sky.
Aryabhata to Nilakantha

Aryabhata (499 CE) stated that Earth rotates on its axis. The Kerala school's Nilakantha Somayaji ( Tantrasamgraha , 1500 CE) proposed that Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn orbit the Sun, which then goes around Earth, a model close to Tycho's, decades before Tycho. Madhava (c. 1350-1425) found infinite series for sine and pi, tools useful for calculating planetary positions.
Key takeaways

Ptolemy's Earth-centred model predicted well but grew complex. Copernicus (1543) made retrograde motion natural with a Sun-centred view. Kepler: ellipses, equal areas, T squared to a cubed. Galileo's telescope gave decisive evidence; Newton explained it all with gravity. Think about it: (1) Why did a simpler model not win immediately? (2) What kind of observation would show that Earth really moves?
Light, Spectra and What Starlight Tells Us
We cannot visit stars, so light is everything

The nearest star beyond the Sun is 4.2 light-years away. No probe will visit in our lifetimes. Yet we know what stars are made of, how hot they are, how fast they move and how they spin. All of it comes from one thing: the light that reaches us.
Light as a wave

Light is an electromagnetic wave. Its wavelength sets its type: radio (metres), microwave, infrared, visible (about 400 nm violet to 700 nm red), ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays (tiny). All travel at the same speed in vacuum: 299,792 km/s . Our eyes see only a thin slice. Astronomers need all of it, because different processes glow in different bands.
Colour tells temperature

Every hot object glows with a smooth rainbow whose peak colour depends on temperature: hotter means bluer. This is blackbody radiation. A red giant (about 3,500 K) looks orange-red; the Sun (about 5,800 K) looks yellow-white; a hot star (above 10,000 K) looks blue-white. Hotter also means far more power: total output goes as temperature to the fourth power (Stefan, 1879).
Spectral lines: a barcode of elements

Pass starlight through a prism or grating and you spread it into a spectrum . Dark gaps, called absorption lines, appear at precise colours. Each element and molecule absorbs only its own colours, like a fingerprint. Joseph von Fraunhofer mapped hundreds of dark lines in sunlight in 1814. In 1859 Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that each line belongs to a chemical element. Suddenly we could do chemistry on the Sun.
Classifying stars

Stars are sorted by line patterns into types O, B, A, F, G, K, M from hottest to coolest. The Sun is G. Annie Jump Cannon built this scheme around 1900. Cecilia Payne then showed in 1925 that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, and that the line patterns differ because of temperature, not composition.
Doppler shift: motion in colour

If a source moves toward us its waves are squeezed: blueshift . If it moves away they are stretched: redshift . The size of the shift gives the speed along the line of sight: v/c = shift in wavelength divided by original wavelength. It reveals binary stars, orbiting planets, spinning galaxies and, as we will see, the expansion of the universe.
Helium was found in the Sun first

During the total solar eclipse of 18 August 1868, the French astronomer Pierre Janssen saw an unfamiliar bright yellow line in the Sun's edge from Guntur in India. Norman Lockyer saw it too; he named the new element helium after the Greek Sun. It was found on Earth only in 1895. A new element discovered 150 million km away.
Be careful

'A star's colour is its composition.' Colour tracks temperature. 'Redshift means the object looks red.' It means its wavelengths are stretched; the object may remain white. 'Light always travels at c.' Only in vacuum. In glass or water it slows down.
Saha, Raman and Guntur

In 1920 Meghnad Saha derived the Saha ionisation equation , showing how a star's temperature and pressure decide which atoms lose electrons. This explained why star types differ and became a foundation of astrophysics. C.V. Raman discovered in 1928 that light scattered by molecules changes colour slightly, the Raman effect , used today to identify materials (Nobel Prize 1930). And the 1868 helium line was first seen from Guntur, Andhra Pradesh.
Key takeaways

All astronomy is decoding light across the electromagnetic spectrum. Colour gives temperature; hotter stars are bluer and much brighter. Spectral lines act as element fingerprints. Doppler shifts give motion along the line of sight. Think about it: (1) Why do two stars of the same temperature but different size have the same colour but different brightness? (2) How could you tell a star is spinning from its spectrum?
Telescopes: From Galileo to JWST
Eyes are tiny buckets of light

Your pupil is about 7 mm wide. A big telescope mirror is metres wide. That collects millions of times more light, so you can see faint, distant objects and fine detail. The history of astronomy is a history of bigger, better light buckets and new colours of vision.
The two jobs of a telescope

First, collecting power : how much light it gathers, proportional to the area of the main lens or mirror (so to diameter squared). Second, resolution : how fine a detail it can separate, which improves with larger diameter and shorter wavelength. Magnification is the least important feature; without light and resolution it only blows up a blur.
Refractors and reflectors

Refractors use lenses. Hans Lippershey patented one in 1608; Galileo built his in 1609. Large lenses sag and give coloured fringes, so the biggest refractor ever is only 1 metre. Reflectors use mirrors. Newton built one in 1668. Mirrors can be supported from behind and made huge. Every major modern telescope is a reflector.
Beyond visible light

Karl Jansky detected radio waves from the Milky Way in 1932, birthing radio astronomy . Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes each show a different universe: cold gas, dust-hidden stars, million-degree gas. Earth's air blocks most of these bands, so many telescopes must fly in space.
Beating the atmosphere

Air blurs stars (twinkling). Fixes: build on high dry mountains (Mauna Kea, the Chilean Atacama, Hanle in Ladakh), use adaptive optics (a deformable mirror that cancels turbulence hundreds of times a second), or go to space. The Hubble Space Telescope (1990, 2.4 m mirror) gave razor-sharp images above the air.
JWST: the infrared giant

The James Webb Space Telescope launched 25 December 2021. It has a 6.5 m mirror of 18 gold-coated beryllium segments and sees infrared, which passes through dust and reveals very distant, redshifted galaxies. It sits near the Sun-Earth L2 point, 1.5 million km from Earth, behind a tennis-court-sized sunshield that keeps it near -233 C. Next: the 39 m Extremely Large Telescope in Chile and the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope.
Interferometry: many dishes, one eye

Link radio dishes across continents and they act like one giant telescope with the resolution of the whole span. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope , linking telescopes around Earth, imaged the shadow of a black hole in galaxy M87. Telescopes now work as a network.
Telescope myths

'The best telescope magnifies most.' Aperture decides. 'Space telescopes are close to the stars.' They are still essentially at Earth's distance; they just avoid the air. 'JWST replaced Hubble.' They complement: different wavelengths.
From Kodaikanal to GMRT and Hanle

The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) near Pune has 30 dishes of 45 m each, built under Govind Swarup and opened in the 1990s: one of the world's most sensitive at low radio frequencies. The 2 m Himalayan Chandra Telescope at Hanle (4,500 m, Ladakh) sits in one of the world's driest, darkest sites. The 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope in Uttarakhand began working in 2016. ISRO's AstroSat (2015) was India's first dedicated astronomy satellite. LIGO-India was approved in 2023.
Key takeaways

Telescopes win on light-collecting area and resolution, not magnification. Reflectors dominate; radio and space telescopes opened other wavelengths. Adaptive optics and orbit beat the atmosphere. JWST sees infrared from L2; networks of dishes can act as one giant telescope. Think about it: (1) Why must infrared telescopes be kept very cold? (2) Why build GMRT in dozens of dishes instead of one huge one?
The Sun
Our star, our only close-up

The Sun holds 99.86 percent of the Solar System's mass, powers almost all life, and is the only star we can study up close. Everything we learn about the Sun is a template for the billions of stars beyond. It also affects us: its storms can disrupt satellites, power grids and radio.
Size, distance, power

Width: 1.39 million km, about 109 Earths side by side. Distance: 150 million km (1 astronomical unit). Light takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to arrive. Age: about 4.6 billion years. It is a middle-sized, middle-aged star, type G. Each second it turns about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy, and releases about 3.8 x 10^26 watts.
Layers from inside out

Core: 15 million K, where fusion happens (next lessons). Radiative zone: energy crawls outward as photons, taking tens of thousands of years or more. Convection zone: hot gas boils up in cells. Photosphere: the visible surface, about 5,800 K. Chromosphere and corona: thin outer atmosphere, the corona exceeds 1 million K, a puzzle: why hotter than the surface?
Sunspots and the 11-year cycle

Sunspots are cooler, darker patches (about 3,800 K) where strong magnetic fields poke through the surface. Heinrich Schwabe noticed in 1843 that their number rises and falls about every 11 years . The magnetic field flips with each cycle, so the full magnetic cycle is about 22 years. Solar Cycle 25 peaked around 2024-2025.
Flares, CMEs and solar wind

Solar flares are sudden bursts of radiation. Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) hurl billions of tonnes of plasma into space. The solar wind is a constant stream of charged particles at 400 to 800 km/s. When a CME hits Earth's magnetic field, it can trigger auroras and geomagnetic storms. The 1859 Carrington Event set telegraph offices on fire. A similar storm today could damage satellites and grids.
The Sun's future

The Sun is slowly brightening, about 10 percent per billion years. In roughly 1 billion years it will be hot enough to boil Earth's oceans. In about 5 billion years it will exhaust core hydrogen, swell into a red giant, shed its layers, and end as a small white dwarf.
Looking inside with sound and neutrinos

Helioseismology studies the Sun's surface vibrations, which are sound waves ringing through its interior, like using earthquakes to image Earth. Solar neutrinos detected underground confirm fusion in the core. Parker Solar Probe (NASA, launched 2018) flew through the corona and in December 2024 passed about 6 million km from the surface.
Sun facts that surprise

'The Sun is burning like a fire.' It is fusion, not chemical burning. 'The Sun is yellow.' It emits white light; the atmosphere makes it look yellow. 'Sunspots are cold holes.' They are cooler than surroundings, but still very bright.
Kodaikanal, Evershed and Aditya-L1

Kodaikanal Solar Observatory (1899) has kept a continuous record of the Sun for over 120 years. There John Evershed found in 1909 that gas flows outward in sunspots, the Evershed effect . ISRO's Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 and reached its halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point, about 1.5 million km away, on 6 January 2024, to study the corona, flares and CMEs with seven instruments including VELC and SUIT.
Key takeaways

The Sun is a G-type star: 15 million K core, 5,800 K surface, hotter corona. Sunspots follow an 11-year cycle driven by magnetism. Flares and CMEs affect space weather on Earth. It will become a red giant in about 5 billion years. Think about it: (1) Why is Aditya-L1 placed at L1 rather than in Earth orbit? (2) What could happen to a modern city after a Carrington-size storm?
Rocky Planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
Four siblings, four different fates

Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars formed from the same cloud, close to the Sun. Yet one is scorched, one is a greenhouse oven, one is alive and one is a frozen desert. Comparing them is how we learn what keeps a planet habitable, a question that matters for our own future and for exoplanets.
What makes them rocky

The inner planets are small and dense, made of rock and metal with thin or no atmospheres. Each has a metal core, a rocky mantle and a crust. They are called terrestrial planets. They formed near the Sun where only rock and metal could stay solid, while lighter gases were blown outward.
Mercury: closest, smallest, extreme

Mercury is only 38 percent of Earth's width, with almost no atmosphere. It circles the Sun in 88 days but spins slowly: three spins in two orbits, so a day from sunrise to sunrise lasts 176 Earth days. Temperatures swing from about 430 C in daylight to -180 C at night. Craters at its poles hold water ice in permanent shadow.
Venus: the runaway greenhouse

Venus is nearly Earth's twin in size, yet its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere (about 90 times Earth's pressure) traps heat: surface 465 C, hotter than Mercury. Sulphuric-acid clouds cover it. It spins backward and so slowly (243 days) that its day is longer than its year (225 days). Early Venus may have had oceans; a runaway greenhouse boiled them away.
Earth: the habitable one

Earth sits in the Sun's habitable zone, where water can be liquid. Other helpers: a magnetic field from its liquid iron core that deflects the solar wind, plate tectonics that recycle carbon and regulate climate, a large Moon that stabilises the axis tilt, and a moderate atmosphere with a greenhouse effect, a gentle one, that keeps the average at about 15 C.
Mars: the lost world

Mars is half Earth's width with 38 percent of Earth's gravity and a thin CO2 atmosphere under 1 percent of Earth's pressure. It has the Solar System's tallest volcano, Olympus Mons (about 22 km), and a canyon system, Valles Marineris , about 4,000 km long. Dry river valleys and minerals show it once had lots of liquid water, 3-4 billion years ago. Its small core cooled, the magnetic field faded, and the solar wind stripped most of its air.
Landers, rovers and orbiters

Mars: Viking landers (1976), then rovers: Curiosity (2012) found ancient lake-bed rock, and Perseverance (landed 18 February 2021) is caching samples in Jezero crater, an ancient river delta. Venus: Soviet Venera landers survived minutes on its surface in the 1970s; Magellan radar-mapped it (1990s). Mercury: NASA's MESSENGER (2011-2015) and the ESA-JAXA BepiColombo mission under way.
Common slips

'Mercury is the hottest planet.' Venus is hotter, due to its greenhouse effect. 'Mars had canals.' Percival Lowell's 1890s 'canals' were optical illusions. 'Greenhouse effect is bad in itself.' Without it Earth would average about -18 C. Too much is the problem, as Venus shows.
Mangalyaan and Venus plans

ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) launched on PSLV on 5 November 2013 and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 , making India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt, at a cost near Rs 450 crore. Its Mars Colour Camera imaged the whole planet. It worked for about eight years. India has approved a Venus Orbiter Mission (Shukrayaan) , planned around 2028.
Key takeaways

Terrestrial planets are small, rocky, with metal cores. Venus is the hottest, from a runaway greenhouse effect. Earth's life-friendly traits: water, magnetic field, tectonics, stable tilt. Mars once had water but lost its air and field. Think about it: (1) What does Venus warn us about greenhouse gases? (2) Why might small planets lose their atmospheres sooner?
Gas and Ice Giants
The planets that rule the Solar System

Jupiter alone has more than twice the mass of all other planets combined. The giants shaped the whole system: they steered comets, sculpted the asteroid belt and probably protected the inner planets. And since giants are the easiest planets to find around other stars, they are the usual face of exoplanets.
Two kinds of giant

Gas giants , Jupiter and Saturn, are mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun, with a small dense core. Ice giants , Uranus and Neptune, are smaller and contain much water, ammonia and methane 'ices' (hot dense fluids, not solid ice) under a hydrogen-helium envelope. Methane absorbs red light, giving Uranus and Neptune their blue-green colour.
Jupiter: the king

Jupiter is 318 times Earth's mass and 11 Earths wide, and spins in under 10 hours. Its bands are cloud stripes in strong winds. The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth, observed for at least 150 years and shrinking. Deep inside, hydrogen is squeezed into a metallic liquid that creates a powerful magnetic field. Orbit: 11.86 years, at 5.2 AU.
Saturn: rings and low density

Saturn is so light for its size that its average density is less than water: it would float in a big enough bathtub. Its rings, made of ice chunks from dust-grain to house size, span 280,000 km but are mostly only about 10 metres thick. Galileo spotted them in 1610 but could not resolve them; Huygens identified them in 1655. Saturn has 274 confirmed moons, after 128 new ones were announced in March 2025.
Uranus and Neptune: the cold edge

Uranus was found by William Herschel in 1781. It is tipped on its side, with an axis tilt of 98 degrees, likely from an ancient collision. Neptune was found in 1846 after Le Verrier and Adams predicted its position from irregularities in Uranus's orbit, a triumph of Newtonian gravity. Neptune has the fastest winds, over 2,000 km/h, even though it receives little sunlight. Voyager 2 is the only probe to visit both (1986, 1989).
Why giants grew big

Beyond the frost line , water ice could form, so there was far more solid material. Jupiter's core grew past about 10 Earth masses and then pulled in huge amounts of gas before the young Sun blew the disc away. Uranus and Neptune formed later or slower and got less gas.
Voyagers, Galileo, Cassini, Juno

Voyager 1 and 2 (launched 1977) toured the giants. Galileo (1995-2003) orbited Jupiter. Cassini (2004-2017) explored Saturn and dropped the Huygens probe on Titan in 2005. Juno (arrived 2016) maps Jupiter's gravity and magnetic field, showing that the core is 'fuzzy' and diluted.
Misunderstandings

'Jupiter is a failed star.' It is about 80 times too light to ignite fusion. 'Only Saturn has rings.' All four giants have rings, Saturn's are simply the brightest. 'Gas giants have a surface.' No; the atmosphere gradually thickens into fluid.
Brihaspati, Shani and Kumbh

In Indian tradition Jupiter is Brihaspati (Guru) and Saturn is Shani . Brihaspati's roughly 12-year orbit (actually 11.86 years) is linked to the timing of the Kumbh Mela cycles in the panchang. Saturn's 29.5-year orbit is the basis of the 'Shani sade-sati' reckoning in traditional astrology. Indian astronomers like Aryabhata and Bhaskara II computed these orbital periods with remarkable accuracy.
Key takeaways

Jupiter and Saturn are mainly hydrogen and helium; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Giants have rings, many moons and no solid surface. The frost line explains why giants formed far out. Neptune was predicted by mathematics before it was seen. Think about it: (1) Why is Saturn less dense than water? (2) How does predicting Neptune from Uranus's wobble resemble finding exoplanets today?
Moons, Rings, Asteroids and Comets
The leftovers that tell the story

Planets get the fame, but moons, asteroids and comets are the preserved building blocks of the Solar System. Some may host life. Some could end it: an asteroid about 10 km wide hit Earth 66 million years ago and ended the dinosaurs.
Moons: worlds of their own

Our Moon is 1/4 of Earth's width. The leading theory: a Mars-size body, Theia , struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago and the debris formed the Moon (giant impact theory). Apollo rocks match Earth's mantle. The Moon's gravity causes tides and steadies Earth's tilt. Other moons: Ganymede (Jupiter) is bigger than Mercury; Io is the most volcanic body known; Europa and Enceladus hide salty oceans under ice; Titan (Saturn) has a thick atmosphere with methane lakes.
Rings

Rings are made of countless small ice or rock bodies orbiting inside the Roche limit , the distance within which a planet's tides tear apart large bodies or stop them from clumping. Saturn's are brightest; Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune have faint ones.
Asteroids

Most asteroids orbit between Mars and Jupiter in the asteroid belt . Despite pictures, it is mostly empty space. The belt's total mass is only about 4 percent of the Moon's. The biggest, Ceres (940 km), is now classed as a dwarf planet. Asteroids are leftover rocks that Jupiter's gravity prevented from forming a planet. Some cross Earth's orbit. In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft hit the small asteroid Dimorphos and changed its orbit, the first test of planetary defence.
Comets: dirty snowballs

A comet is a few-km ball of ice, dust and frozen gases. Near the Sun, it warms; gas and dust stream out as a glowing coma and two tails: a bluish ion tail and a curved dust tail. Tails always point away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, not trailing behind. Short-period comets come from the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune; long-period ones from the Oort cloud , a vast shell of icy bodies. Halley's Comet returns every 76 years (last 1986, next 2061).
Meteors, meteorites and dwarf planets

A meteoroid is a small piece of space rock. When it burns in the air it makes a meteor (shooting star). If it lands, it is a meteorite . Meteor showers happen when Earth crosses a comet's dust trail. Pluto , 2,377 km wide, was reclassified a dwarf planet in 2006 by the IAU because it has not cleared its orbit. New Horizons flew by it in 2015.
Samples

We can hold pieces of these bodies: Apollo moon rocks; Japan's Hayabusa2 returned asteroid Ryugu dust (2020); NASA's OSIRIS-REx brought back asteroid Bennu samples in September 2023; ESA's Rosetta orbited a comet in 2014-2016 and landed a probe. Meteorites reveal the Solar System's age: about 4.57 billion years.
Not quite

'The asteroid belt is dense with rocks.' Spacecraft cross it easily. 'A comet's tail trails behind.' It points away from the Sun. 'Shooting stars are stars.' They are tiny specks burning at about 100 km height.
Chandrayaan, Lonar and a Moon with water

ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 (22 October 2008) carried the Moon Impact Probe and NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper, which found water molecules in the lunar surface in 2009. Chandrayaan-3 landed on 23 August 2023 near the south pole, and its rover measured surface temperatures and detected sulphur. Lonar Lake in Maharashtra is an impact crater in basalt, formed by a meteorite hundreds of thousands of years ago, one of the few such craters in basalt on Earth.
Key takeaways

The Moon likely formed from a giant impact; some moons have oceans and atmospheres. Asteroids are rocky leftovers, mostly in a sparse belt. Comets are icy; tails point away from the Sun. Pluto is a dwarf planet; Kuiper belt and Oort cloud supply comets. Think about it: (1) Why are icy moons good places to search for life? (2) Why did DART matter for humanity?
How the Solar System Formed
A family history with clues

Eight planets orbit in nearly the same plane, in the same direction as the Sun spins. That is not an accident. It is a fingerprint of how the Solar System was born, and the same process now appears to be going on around other young stars.
Start: a collapsing cloud

About 4.6 billion years ago , a cloud of gas and dust, mostly hydrogen and helium plus the ashes of earlier stars, began to collapse under its own gravity, perhaps triggered by a nearby supernova. This is the nebular hypothesis , proposed by Immanuel Kant (1755) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1796).
Spin makes a disc

As the cloud shrank it spun faster, like a skater pulling in her arms (conservation of angular momentum), and flattened into a disc. Most of the mass fell to the centre and became the Sun. The leftover disc, the protoplanetary disc , carried a small fraction of mass, about 1 percent, and almost all the angular momentum. This explains the flat orbits and shared direction.
Dust to planetesimals to planets

Dust grains stuck together, growing into pebbles, then kilometre-size planetesimals , then protoplanets, a process called accretion . In the hot inner disc only rock and metal survived, so rocky planets stayed small. Beyond the frost line (around 3 to 5 AU), ice added mass: giant cores grew and captured gas. Gas giants had only a few million years before the young Sun blew the gas away.
Chaos and migration

The system was violent. Jupiter may have migrated inward and then back out, a model called the Grand Tack, scattering material. Planets collided: Earth was struck by Theia, making the Moon; Uranus may have been knocked over. About 4 billion years ago, a bombardment of leftover bodies cratered the inner planets. Water may have arrived partly from asteroids and comets.
The result
Rocky planets inside, giants outside, a belt of unformed material between Mars and Jupiter, and icy leftovers beyond Neptune. Earth was born about 4.54 billion years ago.
Meteorites, Moon rocks and other discs

Clair Patterson dated meteorites in 1956 using uranium-lead decay: 4.55 billion years. The oldest solid grains (calcium-aluminium inclusions) are 4.567 billion years. Radio telescopes like ALMA now photograph discs around young stars; the 2014 image of HL Tauri shows gaps where baby planets sweep a path. Simple rules predicted exoplanets, but we found surprises, like hot Jupiters, which forced the migration idea.
Small corrections

'Planets formed from a piece torn from the Sun.' That tidal theory fails: they formed from the shared disc. 'Earth was always like this.' It started as molten rock. 'Our system is typical.' Many exoplanet systems look very different.
PRL, meteorites and Narlikar

The Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in Ahmedabad, founded in 1947 by Vikram Sarabhai with K.R. Ramanathan, studies meteorites, isotopes and planetary science, including the PARAS spectrograph that found an exoplanet in 2018. Jayant Narlikar founded IUCAA, Pune, in 1988 to advance research on how cosmic structures form. Chandrayaan lunar data help test impact history, since the Moon preserves the early bombardment.
Key takeaways

The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud. Spin flattened it into a disc, explaining flat, same-direction orbits. The frost line separates rocky and giant planets. Meteorite dating and ALMA images support the model; migration adds the messy details. Think about it: (1) Why do all planets orbit the same way? (2) What would you expect to find around a very young star?
Measuring Stars: Distance, Brightness, the HR Diagram
How far is a point of light?

A star's brightness mixes two things: how powerful it really is, and how far away. To learn anything, astronomers must separate them. Measuring distance is the key step, and a chain of methods, the cosmic distance ladder , builds it from the nearest stars to the edge of the universe.
Parallax: the first rung

Hold a finger out and blink each eye: the finger jumps against the background. In the same way, a nearby star shifts slightly against distant stars as Earth moves around the Sun. The shift angle is its parallax . Friedrich Bessel first measured it in 1838 for 61 Cygni. A star with a parallax of 1 arcsecond is 1 parsec away, about 3.26 light-years . The nearest star system, Alpha Centauri, is 4.37 light-years away, and its faintest member, Proxima Centauri, 4.24. The Gaia satellite has measured parallaxes for nearly two billion stars.
Apparent brightness vs luminosity

Luminosity is a star's true power output. Apparent brightness is how bright it looks from here. Light spreads over a sphere, so brightness falls with the square of distance: twice as far, a quarter as bright (inverse-square law). Astronomers use magnitudes : a lower number means brighter, and 5 magnitudes equals a factor of 100 in brightness. Absolute magnitude is the brightness a star would have at 10 parsecs, so stars can be compared fairly.
Standard candles

Beyond a few thousand light-years parallax fails. We then use objects of known luminosity. Henrietta Leavitt found in 1912 that Cepheid variable stars pulse at a rate linked to their luminosity: slower pulses mean brighter stars. Time the pulse, know the true brightness, compare to apparent brightness, get distance. This ladder rung let Hubble measure Andromeda's distance in 1924.
The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram

Plot stars by temperature (colour) against luminosity and they do not scatter: they fall into groups. This is the HR diagram (Hertzsprung 1911, Russell 1913). Main sequence: a diagonal band holding about 90 percent of stars, including the Sun, all fusing hydrogen. Red giants: cool but huge, so bright. White dwarfs: hot but tiny, so faint.
Mass decides everything

On the main sequence, position tells mass. Heavy stars are hot, blue and extremely bright but live short lives (millions of years). Light red dwarfs are dim but live for trillions of years. Luminosity rises roughly as mass to the power 3.5. The Sun is a middle-ranking star with a ten-billion-year life.
Ladder checks

Each rung of the distance ladder is calibrated by the one below: parallax calibrates Cepheids, Cepheids calibrate supernovae. Independent methods agree to a few percent, and Gaia has tightened the bottom rung.
Watch out

'The brightest-looking star is the closest or the biggest.' It may just be powerful, or near. 'A larger magnitude means brighter.' It is the opposite. 'Stars on the HR diagram are moving along it all the time.' They move over millions to billions of years, not days.
Bappu-Wilson and Saha

Vainu Bappu , builder of the Kavalur observatory, with Olin Wilson found in 1957 the Bappu-Wilson effect : the width of a calcium emission line in cool stars tells how luminous they are, giving a new distance tool. The Vainu Bappu Telescope (2.34 m) in Tamil Nadu is named after him. Meghnad Saha's work (1920) connected spectral type to temperature, which underpins the HR diagram.
Key takeaways

Parallax gives distances to nearby stars; Cepheids extend the ladder. Brightness falls with distance squared; lower magnitude is brighter. The HR diagram groups stars by temperature and luminosity. Mass sets a star's position and lifetime. Think about it: (1) Why do massive stars die sooner despite having more fuel? (2) Why can't parallax measure distance to other galaxies?
How Stars Shine: Nuclear Fusion
What keeps a star from collapsing or exploding

A star is a balancing act. Gravity squeezes it inwards. Pressure from hot gas pushes outward. Fusion in the core supplies the heat that keeps the balance. Understanding fusion explained how the Sun has shone for billions of years, a puzzle that stumped 19th century physicists.
The age puzzle

Lord Kelvin calculated that if the Sun were just shrinking under gravity, it could shine for only about 20 million years. But geology and fossils said Earth was far older. Chemical burning would last only thousands of years. A new energy source was needed.
E = mc squared

In 1905 Einstein showed that mass is a form of energy: E = mc squared. A tiny bit of mass becomes a huge amount of energy because c squared is enormous. In 1920 Arthur Eddington proposed that stars convert hydrogen to helium. Four hydrogen nuclei weigh slightly more than one helium nucleus; the 0.7 percent difference is released as energy.
The proton-proton chain

In the Sun, protons fuse in steps: two protons form deuterium (a proton turns into a neutron, emitting a neutrino); deuterium plus a proton makes helium-3; two helium-3 nuclei make helium-4 and release two protons. The Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second, losing about 4 million tonnes of mass as energy. Hans Bethe worked out these steps (and the CNO cycle in heavier stars) in 1939 and won the Nobel Prize in 1967.
Why the temperature is not enough

Protons repel each other. Classical physics says even 15 million K is too cold for them to touch. Quantum mechanics rescues the idea: particles can tunnel through the barrier with small probability (George Gamow, 1928). The Sun's fusion is slow but there are so many protons that it works. That slowness is why the Sun lasts about 10 billion years.
Balance, and what happens when fuel runs low

If fusion speeds up, the core expands and cools, slowing fusion: a thermostat. When hydrogen runs out in the core, the core contracts and heats, the outer layers swell, and the star leaves the main sequence. Heavier stars go on to fuse helium to carbon and oxygen, then heavier elements up to iron , which releases no energy when fused.
Neutrinos from the core

Photons from the core need tens of thousands of years or more to random-walk out, but neutrinos fly straight out in 2 seconds. Raymond Davis's Homestake experiment (1960s) detected only about a third of the predicted neutrinos: the 'solar neutrino problem'. It was solved when neutrinos were shown to change type in flight (Nobel Prize 2015, Kajita and McDonald), confirming the Sun's fusion model.
Mistakes to avoid

'Stars burn like fire.' Burning needs oxygen; fusion does not. 'The Sun will explode as a bomb.' It will not; its fusion is self-regulating. 'Fusion is easy to copy.' On Earth it needs 100 million degrees and intense confinement.
Fusion research at home

India is a member of ITER , the international fusion experiment in France (joined 2005). The Institute for Plasma Research in Gandhinagar runs the SST-1 tokamak, India's superconducting steady-state fusion device. Scientists like Meghnad Saha (ionisation of stellar gas) and Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (stellar structure) laid foundations for this field.
Key takeaways

Stars shine by fusing hydrogen to helium, turning 0.7 percent of mass into energy. Quantum tunnelling makes fusion possible at 15 million K. Pressure from fusion balances gravity, a stable thermostat. Neutrino detection confirmed solar fusion. Think about it: (1) Why does a heavier star burn out faster? (2) Why does fusing iron not power a star?
Birth of Stars: Nebulae and Protostars
Stars are being born right now

Stars live for millions to trillions of years, so we cannot watch one grow. But the sky holds stars of every age at once, like a forest with seedlings and old trees. In the Milky Way about one to two new Sun-like stars form each year, in dark, cold clouds.
Molecular clouds: the nurseries

Stars form in molecular clouds : cold (about 10 K), dense clouds of hydrogen gas (as H2 molecules) and dust, weighing thousands to millions of Suns. Dust blocks starlight, so they look like black patches, e.g. the Horsehead Nebula. In them the gas is cold enough that gravity can beat the pressure.
Collapse begins

A part of the cloud, nudged by a shockwave from a nearby supernova, a collision of clouds or a passing spiral arm, becomes dense enough that gravity wins. This is the Jeans instability . The clump falls inward and fragments into many cores, which is why stars are born in clusters , like the Pleiades.
Protostar and disc

Collapsing material heats up. A hot, glowing, not-yet-fusing core forms: a protostar . Spin flattens the surrounding material into a disc and it also launches two jets along the axis, which carry away spin. The disc feeds the star and later forms planets, as in lesson 1-0-4.
Ignition and mass limits

When the core reaches about 10 million K , hydrogen fusion starts and the star joins the main sequence. If the object is lighter than about 0.08 Suns (80 Jupiters), the core never gets hot enough for hydrogen fusion; it becomes a brown dwarf . At the top, stars above roughly 100 Suns are rare because radiation tears them up. Small stars are much more common than large ones.
Radiation and feedback

Newborn massive stars blow winds and ionising light that carve cavities and may stop further star formation, or compress neighbouring gas and trigger it. The famous Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula (Hubble 1995, JWST 2022) are towers of gas being eroded by such stars.
Seeing through dust

Visible light cannot pass through dense dust, but infrared and radio can. The Orion Nebula , about 1,350 light-years away and visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy 'star' in Orion's sword, holds stars at all ages. Spitzer , Herschel , ALMA and JWST reveal protostars, discs and jets, matching the theory.
Clearing up

'Nebulae are just pretty clouds.' They are both nurseries and graveyards. 'A star forms in one go.' Formation takes up to a few million years. 'Brown dwarfs are planets.' They are heavier than planets but too light to be true stars.
Mriga, Orion and radio hydrogen

In Indian tradition Orion is Mriga , the deer, with Mrigashira a nakshatra; the three stars of Orion's belt were seen as an arrow aimed at it. The GMRT maps cold hydrogen gas through the 21 cm radio line, tracing the gas that forms stars. ISRO's AstroSat Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope has studied young hot stars in star clusters and galaxies.
Key takeaways

Stars form from cold, dense molecular clouds that collapse under gravity. A protostar with a disc and jets forms first; fusion starts at about 10 million K. Below 0.08 solar masses, an object is a brown dwarf. Infrared and radio let us see inside nurseries like Orion. Think about it: (1) Why are stars often born in groups? (2) Why do hot young stars end up destroying their own nursery?
Death of Stars: White Dwarfs and Supernovae
We are made of dead stars

The hydrogen and most helium in the universe came from the Big Bang. Nearly everything else, the carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe, the calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, was made inside stars and scattered when they died. Stellar death is also the source of black holes and neutron stars.
Fate depends on mass

Stars below about 8 Suns end quietly as white dwarfs; those above about 8 Suns end in a supernova. The less massive the star, the slower and gentler the death. Red dwarfs will take trillions of years; none has yet died.
Red giant and planetary nebula

When hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats and hydrogen burns in a shell around it. The outer layers swell and cool: a red giant . In about 5 billion years the Sun will reach near Earth's present orbit. The star later puffs off its outer layers as a glowing shell, called a planetary nebula (a misleading name from early telescopes; they have nothing to do with planets).
White dwarf: a cooling Earth-sized star

What remains is the hot core: a white dwarf , the mass of the Sun in a body the size of Earth. A teaspoon would weigh several tonnes. It no longer fuses; it only cools slowly. It is held up not by heat but by electron degeneracy pressure , a quantum effect of crowded electrons.
The Chandrasekhar limit

In 1930, aged 19, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated that this quantum pressure can only hold up a white dwarf of up to about 1.4 Suns . Heavier, and gravity wins. This Chandrasekhar limit was fiercely disputed by Eddington, but proved right, and earned Chandrasekhar the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Two kinds of supernova

Type Ia: a white dwarf in a binary pulls gas from its partner, or merges with another, until it nears 1.4 Suns and detonates as a thermonuclear explosion. All explode with nearly the same brightness, so they serve as standard candles for cosmic distances. Core-collapse (Type II): a massive star's iron core can no longer be supported; in under a second it collapses to a neutron star or black hole while the outer layers bounce off and explode, briefly outshining a whole galaxy.
Cosmic recycling

Supernovae forge and spread elements heavier than iron too. Gold and platinum come largely from neutron star collisions (confirmed in 2017). The ejected material seeds new nebulae, which form new stars and planets enriched with heavy elements: our Solar System is a third-generation product.
Records of exploding stars

Chinese astronomers recorded the 1054 CE 'guest star' that left the Crab Nebula . Tycho (1572) and Kepler (1604) saw supernovae in our galaxy; none since. SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud was seen in February 1987, and neutrinos from its core were detected on Earth hours before the light, confirming core collapse.
Be careful

'The Sun will go supernova.' It is too light. 'A supernova is a new star.' It is the death of one. The Latin name nova means new, from old naming. 'White dwarfs are tiny in mass.' They hold roughly a Sun's mass.
Chandrasekhar, Lahore to Chicago

Chandrasekhar was born in Lahore (1910), nephew of C.V. Raman, and studied at Presidency College, Madras. On the ship to England in 1930 he worked out the mass limit of white dwarfs. He spent his career at the University of Chicago; NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory (1999) is named for him. In India, AstroSat studies supernova remnants in X-rays.
Key takeaways

Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs; stars over about 8 Suns explode. The Chandrasekhar limit, 1.4 Suns, caps a white dwarf's mass. Type Ia supernovae are standard candles; Type II create neutron stars or black holes. Supernovae spread heavy elements that build planets and life. Think about it: (1) Why are Type Ia explosions so similar? (2) What does 'we are star dust' mean in physics terms?
Neutron Stars and Pulsars
Matter at its limit

A neutron star is what is left when a massive star's core collapses: more than a Sun's mass in a ball about 20 km across, the size of a city. It is the densest object we can directly observe apart from black holes, a natural laboratory for physics we cannot recreate on Earth.
Making a neutron star

During a core-collapse supernova, gravity crushes the core so hard that electrons and protons merge into neutrons . The collapse stops when neutrons crowd so tightly that quantum neutron degeneracy pressure resists. The typical mass is 1.4 to about 2 Suns in a radius of 10 km. Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky predicted them in 1934, just two years after the neutron's discovery.
Extreme numbers

Density: about 10^17 kg per cubic metre. A teaspoon would weigh around a billion tonnes. Gravity at the surface is hundreds of billions of times Earth's. An escape speed around half the speed of light. Magnetic fields up to a trillion times Earth's; a magnetar reaches 10^14 to 10^15 gauss, strong enough to disrupt atoms.
Spinning fast

Like a skater drawing in her arms, a collapsing core spins faster. A neutron star may spin tens or hundreds of times a second. The Crab pulsar spins about 30 times a second. The fastest known, 716 times a second, is a millisecond pulsar , spun up by gas from a companion.
Pulsars: cosmic lighthouses

A neutron star's powerful magnetic field funnels radio beams from its magnetic poles. If the magnetic axis is tilted from the spin axis, the beam sweeps around, and if it crosses Earth we see regular pulses , each time the beam passes.
Why pulsars are clocks

Millisecond pulsars tick with stability rivalling atomic clocks. Astronomers use them to detect tiny disturbances in space-time and to test gravity. Binary pulsars confirmed Einstein's prediction that orbiting masses lose energy as gravitational waves (Hulse and Taylor, 1974, Nobel 1993). A global network, the pulsar timing array , reported in 2023 evidence of a gravitational-wave background.
The discovery of pulsars

In November 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell , working at Cambridge with Antony Hewish, noticed a faint signal pulsing every 1.337 seconds. It was so regular they half-jokingly called it LGM-1 ('little green men'). They soon found more. Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics, a choice widely thought to have unfairly left out Bell Burnell. The Crab pulsar was found in 1968, linking pulsars to supernovae.
Quick corrections

'Pulsars blink on and off.' The star shines steadily; the beam sweeps past us. 'Neutron stars are made of ordinary neutrons in a nucleus.' They are one enormous nuclear-density object, with exotic matter possibly inside. 'Pulsars are alien signals.' Natural, though first mistaken for one.
Ooty, GMRT and the Indian pulsar timing

The Ooty Radio Telescope (1970), built by the Tata Institute under Govind Swarup, a 530 m long cylindrical dish on a hillside tilted to line up with Earth's axis, was used for early pulsar and lunar-occultation studies. The GMRT finds and times pulsars; the Indian Pulsar Timing Array (InPTA) joined the 2023 global announcement of a nanohertz gravitational-wave background. AstroSat has observed the Crab pulsar in X-rays.
Key takeaways

Neutron stars are collapsed stellar cores about 20 km across and 1.4 to 2 Suns in mass. Pulsars are spinning, magnetised neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth. They are precise clocks that test gravity and detect gravitational waves. Jocelyn Bell found the first in 1967. Think about it: (1) Why must a neutron star spin so fast after collapse? (2) What would it mean if a pulsar's ticks suddenly shifted?
Black Holes
Gravity at its extreme

A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. It is the logical end of Einstein's general relativity, and the best place to test it. It also anchors the centre of most big galaxies and powers the brightest objects in the universe.
An old idea, a new theory

In 1783 John Michell, and later Laplace, wondered: if a star were massive enough, its escape speed would exceed the speed of light and it would be dark. Einstein's general relativity (1915) turned this into a theory. In 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found the exact solution, giving a radius at which escape is impossible.
Size and the event horizon

The Schwarzschild radius is r = 2GM/c squared. For the Sun it is about 3 km; for Earth about 9 mm. If the Sun were squeezed into a ball of 3 km, it would be a black hole. The surface at that radius is the event horizon : a one-way door. Cross it and no signal can return.
Inside the horizon

At the centre, general relativity predicts a singularity , where density and curvature become infinite, a sign that the theory breaks down and quantum gravity is needed. Near a stellar-mass black hole, tides stretch you like spaghetti. Distant observers see a falling clock slow down and fade at the horizon, though the faller notices nothing special when crossing a large horizon.
Types and formation

Stellar-mass (a few to tens of Suns): from collapsing massive stars. Supermassive (millions to billions of Suns): in galaxy centres. Our Milky Way's Sagittarius A* has about 4 million Suns; M87's about 6.5 billion. Intermediate : a few thousand Suns, now being found. How supermassive ones grew so large so early is a live question.
Seeing the unseen

A black hole emits no light, but matter spiralling in forms a hot accretion disc that glows in X-rays, and jets can blaze across a galaxy. Cygnus X-1 (1971) was the first strong candidate. Stars orbiting the Milky Way's centre revealed Sgr A*; this won the 2020 Nobel Prize (Genzel and Ghez), shared with Roger Penrose for proving that black holes follow from relativity (1965).
Hawking radiation

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that quantum effects near the horizon make black holes emit a faint glow and slowly lose mass. For a stellar-mass hole it is far too small to detect and the lifetime is vastly longer than the universe's age. It links gravity, quantum theory and thermodynamics.
Images and ripples

In 2015 LIGO heard two black holes merge. In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole shadow, M87*, and in May 2022 one of Sgr A*, in our own galaxy. Both matched Einstein's predictions.
Not vacuum cleaners

'Black holes suck in everything.' If the Sun became a black hole of equal mass, Earth would keep orbiting normally. 'They are holes.' They are objects with mass. 'Nobody has seen one.' We have images and gravitational-wave detections.
Chandrasekhar, Raychaudhuri and AstroSat

The Chandrasekhar limit (1930) showed that heavy enough stars cannot stop collapsing: the first step to black holes. Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri derived in 1955 the Raychaudhuri equation , a key ingredient in the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems. ISRO's AstroSat found in 2017 rapid X-ray pulsations in the black hole system GRS 1915+105 and studied Cygnus X-1.
Key takeaways

A black hole is a region of no escape, bounded by an event horizon of radius 2GM/c squared. Stellar ones come from massive stars; supermassive ones sit in galaxy centres. We detect them by accretion light, orbiting stars, gravitational waves and shadow images. Hawking radiation hints at a link with quantum physics. Think about it: (1) Why would the Sun, as a black hole, not change Earth's orbit? (2) Why is the singularity a sign of incomplete physics?
Exoplanets and the Search for Life
Are we alone?

Until 1992 we knew of planets around only one star: ours. Now we know of over 6,000 confirmed planets around other stars (as of 2025) and have learned that planets are more common than stars. The question of life elsewhere has moved from philosophy to measurement.
Why planets are hard to see

A planet is millions to billions of times fainter than its star and lies very close to it. It is like trying to see a firefly beside a searchlight from thousands of kilometres. So astronomers mostly detect planets by their effect on the star's light or motion.
Transit method

When a planet crosses in front of its star, the starlight dips by a tiny fraction, e.g. about 1 percent for a Jupiter and 0.01 percent for an Earth. Regular repeating dips reveal the planet's size and orbit. NASA's Kepler telescope (2009-2018) found thousands this way; TESS (2018) hunts nearby stars.
Wobble method

A planet tugs its star; the star wobbles about the shared centre of mass. The wobble shows up as a back-and-forth Doppler shift in the star's spectrum (radial velocity). In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b , a Jupiter-size planet orbiting every 4.2 days, the first around a Sun-like star (Nobel 2019). Earlier, in 1992, Wolszczan and Frail found planets around a pulsar.
Other methods and the zoo

Direct imaging blocks the star and photographs young, hot, distant giants. Microlensing uses a star's gravity to magnify a background star. The zoo is wild: hot Jupiters hugging their stars, super-Earths (the commonest type, none in our system), lava worlds and planets orbiting two suns. Our Solar System is not the template.
The habitable zone

The habitable zone is the range of distances where a rocky planet could have liquid water on its surface. It depends on the star's brightness: close in for dim red dwarfs, farther for bright stars. TRAPPIST-1 , a red dwarf 40 light-years away, has seven Earth-size planets, three in or near the zone. Proxima b orbits the nearest star. Being in the zone does not guarantee habitability.
Looking for biosignatures

When a planet transits, a tiny bit of starlight passes through its atmosphere, and gases leave spectral fingerprints. JWST can now read these. Researchers look for gases like oxygen, methane and carbon dioxide together, which would be hard to explain without life. Claims, such as hints of dimethyl sulphide on the sub-Neptune K2-18 b (2023, 2025), did not survive reanalysis: 2025 studies found no reliable signal, though the methane detection stands. Closer to home, Mars, Europa and Enceladus are targets for life search.
The numbers game

The Drake equation (Frank Drake, 1961) multiplies factors: stars, fraction with planets, habitable ones, fraction with life, intelligence and technology, longevity. We now know the planet factors well, but not the biology. The Fermi paradox asks: if intelligent life is common, where is everybody? SETI listens for artificial radio signals; nothing confirmed so far.
Not what you may think

'We have found life elsewhere.' No. No detection is confirmed. 'Habitable zone means inhabited.' It only means liquid water is possible. 'Exoplanet pictures are photos.' Most are artist's impressions of data.
PARAS and the first Indian exoplanet

In 2018 the PARAS spectrograph at PRL's Mount Abu observatory helped confirm EPIC 211945201 b (K2-236 b), a planet about 27 times Earth's mass, 600 light-years away: the first exoplanet discovered with an Indian telescope. Indian scientists work on JWST data analysis, and ISRO's AstroSat and future missions add to the planetary and biosignature search. India's Mangalyaan, Chandrayaan and the planned Venus mission also probe habitability in our own system.
Key takeaways

Over 6,000 exoplanets are confirmed (as of 2025); planets are common. Main methods: transit and radial velocity; also imaging and microlensing. Habitable zone means liquid water is possible, not guaranteed. JWST reads atmospheres for biosignatures; no life has been confirmed. Think about it: (1) Why are transits only seen for some planets? (2) What would make a biosignature convincing rather than a false alarm?
The Milky Way
Our home address

The band of light across a dark sky is where we look edge-on through our own galaxy. We live inside it, so mapping it is like mapping a forest from within. Learning its shape, size and our place in it was one of the great steps in astronomy.
What the band is

Galileo saw in 1610 that the Milky Way band breaks into countless faint stars. It is the combined glow of our galaxy's disc, seen from inside. The name Milky Way is old; the Greek word gave us 'galaxy'.
Shape and size

The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy : a flat disc about 100,000 light-years across and only about 1,000 thick, a central bulge with a bar of stars, and spiral arms where gas and young stars concentrate. It has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars and a diffuse halo of old stars and globular clusters.
Our position

The Sun lies in a minor arm, the Orion Arm (Orion Spur), about 26,000 light-years from the centre. It orbits at about 230 km/s and takes roughly 225 to 250 million years for one lap, a 'galactic year'. Since the Sun formed it has made about 20 laps. The Solar System also bobs up and down through the disc.
The centre: a supermassive black hole

Dust hides the centre in visible light, but infrared and radio reveal it. Stars at the centre orbit an invisible object, Sagittarius A* , with about 4 million Suns. One star, S2, whips around it every 16 years. In May 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope imaged its shadow.
Rotation and a hint of dark matter

Stars in the outer disc orbit surprisingly fast, not slowing down with distance as planets in the Solar System do. Visible matter cannot supply enough gravity. That points to a massive halo of dark matter , which holds about 5 to 10 times the mass of all the stars. See lesson 3-0-2.
Mapping from the inside

William Herschel (1785) counted stars and wrongly placed the Sun near the centre. In 1918 Harlow Shapley mapped globular clusters, found that they centre on a point far away in Sagittarius, and so showed that the Sun is off-centre. In 1920 the Shapley-Curtis debate asked if spiral 'nebulae' were separate galaxies; Hubble settled it in 1924 with Cepheids in Andromeda. Gaia now gives 3D positions and motions for nearly two billion stars.
Common mix-ups

'The Milky Way is the universe.' It is one of hundreds of billions of galaxies. 'Stars in the band are all nearby.' The band holds stars up to tens of thousands of light-years away. 'We are at the centre.' We are about halfway out. The Milky Way and Andromeda will merge in billions of years, though estimates of timing and certainty are being revised.
Akashganga and the GMRT

In Sanskrit and Hindi the Milky Way is Akashganga , the river of the sky, and it appears in many stories. India's GMRT maps the 21 cm hydrogen line to trace gas in spiral arms, and AstroSat studies star clusters across the galaxy in ultraviolet. The lunar nakshatras and the Saptarishi all lie in our local Milky Way neighbourhood.
Key takeaways

The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy of 100 to 400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun is 26,000 light-years from the centre and orbits in about 230 million years. Sgr A*, about 4 million Suns, sits at the centre. Rotation speeds point to a dark matter halo. Think about it: (1) Why was it so hard to learn our galaxy's shape? (2) What would the sky look like if we lived near the galactic centre?
Galaxies, Clusters and the Cosmic Web
The universe is made of galaxies

Beyond the Milky Way there are hundreds of billions of galaxies, each with millions to trillions of stars. They are the building blocks of the cosmos. Their arrangement, in clumps, chains and voids, preserves the pattern laid down in the early universe.
Shapes of galaxies

Edwin Hubble's 1926 classification still helps: Spirals : a flat rotating disc with arms, rich in gas and young blue stars (Milky Way, Andromeda). Ellipticals : smooth balls of old red stars, little gas. Irregulars : shapeless, often small, with active star formation.
How big, how many

Galaxies range from dwarfs with a few million stars to giants with trillions. Andromeda (M31) , 2.5 million light-years away, is the nearest big galaxy and the farthest object visible to the naked eye. The Hubble Deep Field (1995) pointed at a seemingly empty patch and revealed about 3,000 galaxies; JWST sees galaxies from just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.
Groups and clusters

Galaxies rarely live alone. The Local Group holds about 80 galaxies, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda, with the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds as satellites. The Virgo Cluster , about 55 million light-years away, has over 1,000 galaxies. Rich clusters hold hundreds to thousands, bound by gravity.
Superclusters, filaments and voids

On the largest scales, galaxies form filaments and sheets surrounding giant empty voids , a pattern like soap foam, called the cosmic web . The Great Wall (Geller and Huchra, 1989) is a sheet about 500 million light-years long. In 2014 Brent Tully's team mapped our home supercluster, Laniakea , about 500 million light-years across and flowing toward a gravitational attractor.
Galaxy evolution

Galaxies grow by merging. Spirals colliding can form ellipticals. The Milky Way has eaten dwarf galaxies. When gas funnels onto a central black hole, the galaxy's core becomes an active galactic nucleus or quasar (first identified by Maarten Schmidt in 1963), billions of times brighter than the Sun.
Seeing the web

Redshift surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, turn galaxy positions and redshifts into 3D maps. Gravity, acting on tiny early irregularities, pulled matter into this web, and computer simulations (Millennium, Illustris) reproduce it only when dark matter is included.
Be careful

'Galaxies are evenly spread.' They cluster into a web. 'Galaxies collide like billiard balls.' Stars are so far apart that few actually collide. 'Distant galaxies are young now.' We see them as they were; they look young because their light is old.
IUCAA and the Saraswati Supercluster

The Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA) in Pune, founded in 1988 by Jayant Narlikar , is a hub of galaxy research. In 2017 an IUCAA-led team (with Joydeep Bagchi) announced the Saraswati Supercluster , a giant structure of over 40 galaxy clusters, about 600 million light-years across and about 4 billion light-years away. The uGMRT and AstroSat study galaxy evolution; the UVIT detected the ultraviolet light of one of the most distant galaxies, AUDFs01, in 2021.
Key takeaways

Galaxies are spiral, elliptical or irregular, containing millions to trillions of stars. They gather in groups, clusters and superclusters. Large-scale structure is a cosmic web of filaments around voids. Mergers and central black holes drive galaxy evolution. Think about it: (1) Why would computer models need dark matter to make the web? (2) What does seeing a distant galaxy tell us about the past?
Dark Matter
Most of the matter is missing

The stars, gas and dust that we see, everything made of atoms, make up only about 5 percent of the universe's energy. About 27 percent is dark matter , which does not emit or absorb light but pulls with gravity. About 68 percent is dark energy. Dark matter outweighs ordinary matter by about 5 to 1.
First clue: clusters (1933)

Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured how fast galaxies move in the Coma Cluster. They moved so quickly that the cluster should fly apart unless it contained far more mass than the visible stars. He called the missing stuff dunkle Materie , dark matter. Few took it seriously.
Strong clue: spinning galaxies

In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast stars and gas orbit in spiral galaxies, starting with Andromeda. If only visible matter existed, outer stars would orbit slower, as outer planets do. Instead the speeds stay flat out to the edges. Something invisible fills a huge halo around each galaxy.
Gravitational lensing

Einstein's theory says mass bends light. A cluster of galaxies acts like a lens, distorting images of galaxies behind it. The amount of bending tells us the total mass, which is far larger than the visible stuff. In the Bullet Cluster (2006 analysis) two colliding clusters show the lensing mass lying separately from the hot gas, direct evidence that the mass is not ordinary gas.
Evidence from the early universe

The pattern of ripples in the cosmic microwave background and the growth of the cosmic web both need dark matter. Without it gravity could not pull matter into galaxies in 13.8 billion years. Ordinary matter alone would be too smooth.
What could it be?

It is not ordinary atoms, and not neutrinos (too light and fast). Candidates: WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles), axions (very light particles), or primordial black holes. Large underground detectors (XENON, LUX-ZEPLIN) have found no clear WIMP signal. Another idea, MOND (Milgrom, 1983), modifies gravity instead, but struggles to explain clusters and the CMB.
Many independent lines

Galaxy rotation, galaxy clusters, lensing, the CMB, and cosmic structure all agree on the same amount, a rare case where unrelated methods converge. That is why most astronomers accept dark matter, even though we do not know what it is.
Not what it sounds like

'Dark matter is black holes or dust.' Ordinary dark objects are limited by other measurements. 'Dark matter and dark energy are the same.' They are different: one clumps and attracts, the other drives acceleration. 'Scientists invented it to save a theory.' It was forced by measurements, and tested many ways.
Deep underground and lensing

India has a history in deep-underground particle physics: in 1965 TIFR's detectors in the Kolar Gold Fields mine, 2 km deep, recorded the first atmospheric neutrinos. A proposed India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) in Tamil Nadu's Theni district has faced delays. Researchers at IUCAA and TIFR work on gravitational lensing and large-scale structure, and on simulations that include dark matter.
Key takeaways

Dark matter is about 27 percent of the universe and 85 percent of its matter. Evidence: galaxy rotation curves, cluster speeds, lensing, CMB, structure growth. It does not interact with light; its identity is unknown. WIMPs, axions and modified gravity are candidate explanations. Think about it: (1) Why do flat rotation curves need extra mass? (2) What kind of observation could rule out WIMPs?
The Expanding Universe: Hubble and Redshift
The universe has a history

For most of history people assumed the universe was eternal and unchanging. In the 1920s the evidence showed otherwise: galaxies are flying apart. If they move apart now, they were closer before. Winding the film back leads to a beginning, the Big Bang.
Slipher and the redshifts
