Between 1912 and 1920s, Vesto Slipher measured spectra of spiral 'nebulae' and found most were redshifted: moving away fast. Their speeds were far greater than the stars in our galaxy. The nature of the nebulae was still debated.
Hubble settles the scale (1924 to 1929)

In 1924 Edwin Hubble found Cepheid variables in Andromeda and showed it lay about a million light-years away (the modern value is about 2.5 million), well outside the Milky Way: these were separate galaxies. In 1929 he combined distances with redshifts and found that the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes .
Hubble-Lemaitre law

The relation is v = H0 x d : recession speed v equals distance d times the Hubble constant H0, now about 70 km/s per megaparsec. A galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7,000 km/s. Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and physicist, predicted and estimated this in 1927 from Einstein's equations, two years before Hubble. In 2018 the IAU voted to call it the Hubble-Lemaitre law .
Space itself expands

Galaxies are not flying through space from a centre. Space itself is stretching , like dots on an inflating balloon or raisins in rising dough: from any raisin, all others recede, and the farther ones faster. So there is no centre and no edge. Light waves are stretched along the way, producing cosmological redshift , which differs from the ordinary Doppler shift.
Redshift z and the age

Redshift z measures the stretch: 1 + z is the factor by which the universe has expanded since the light left. A galaxy at z = 1 is seen when the universe was half its present size. Running the expansion backward, 1/H0 gives roughly 14 billion years , close to the real age, 13.8 billion years.
Two numbers that disagree

Measuring H0 is hard. Cepheids and supernovae in nearby galaxies (the SH0ES team, Adam Riess) give about 73 km/s/Mpc. The CMB analysed with the standard model (Planck) gives about 67 to 68. This Hubble tension is over 5 sigma, and may be a hint of new physics or hidden errors. It remains unresolved as of 2025.
Careful here

'Galaxies fly away from a centre.' There is no centre. 'Everything expands, including us.' Gravity or electromagnetic forces hold galaxies, atoms and you together; only the space between clusters grows. 'Redshift always means motion through space.' At great distances it is stretching of space.
Narlikar and rival ideas

Jayant Narlikar worked with Fred Hoyle on the steady-state and the Hoyle-Narlikar gravity theories, rivals to the Big Bang. The CMB evidence settled the debate in favour of the Big Bang, but the rival ideas pushed the field to test hard. IUCAA and TIFR astronomers analyse supernova and galaxy-survey data to measure expansion. The uGMRT maps redshifted hydrogen emission from distant galaxies.
Key takeaways

Galaxies recede with speeds proportional to distance: v = H0 x d. Space itself stretches; there is no centre of expansion. Redshift measures how much the universe has grown since the light left. The Hubble tension shows two methods disagree on H0. Think about it: (1) Why does the law imply a beginning? (2) Why do galaxies not expand with space?
The Big Bang and the Cosmic Microwave Background
The origin story with receipts

The Big Bang is not a guess or a myth: it is the best-tested account of our beginning. It predicts how much helium exists, the temperature of the sky and the pattern of the ripples on it, and all three match. Here is the story and the evidence.
What the Big Bang is, and is not

It was not an explosion in space . It was the rapid expansion of space itself from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago . There is no centre to point to; it happened everywhere. The theory describes what happened after the first fraction of a second; the very first instant is unknown.
Timeline of a cooling universe

Inflation (Alan Guth, 1981) may have stretched the universe enormously in the first 10^-32 seconds. After about a microsecond, quarks bind into protons and neutrons. Between about 3 and 20 minutes, Big Bang nucleosynthesis fuses hydrogen into helium and a little lithium: the universe ends up with about 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium by mass . At about 380,000 years , it cools to about 3,000 K and electrons join nuclei into atoms.
The first light

Before that, the universe was an opaque glowing fog of charged particles that scattered light. When atoms formed, light was free to travel, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) . Since then, expansion has stretched its wavelength 1,100 times, from visible light to microwaves, with a temperature of 2.725 K . Every cubic centimetre of space holds about 411 of these photons.
Discovery of the CMB

George Gamow, Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman predicted it around 1948. In 1964 to 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs found an unexplained hiss in their antenna that came from all directions, even after cleaning out pigeon droppings. They had found the afterglow (Nobel 1978). In 1992 COBE showed it matches a perfect blackbody (Mather and Smoot, Nobel 2006).
Ripples: seeds of galaxies

The CMB is smooth to about 1 part in 100,000, but the tiny temperature differences are the seeds: denser patches that gravity grew into galaxies and clusters. WMAP (2001) and Planck (2009 to 2013) mapped them in detail. The ripple pattern gives the universe's age, shape (flat) and composition: about 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter, 68 percent dark energy.
Three pillars

Expansion of galaxies (Hubble). CMB : its temperature and blackbody spectrum. Light element abundances : helium about 25 percent matches nucleosynthesis theory. JWST has found surprisingly bright, early galaxies, which refines, but does not overturn, the picture.
Clearing the air

'The Big Bang happened at one point in space.' It happened everywhere. 'The universe expands into something.' The model does not need an outside. 'The CMB is a leftover from an explosion.' It is light released when atoms formed.
Narlikar, IUCAA and SARAS

Indian scientists contributed to the debate and the data. Jayant Narlikar promoted alternatives, keeping the field honest. IUCAA scientists analyse CMB data from Planck. In 2022 the SARAS 3 radio experiment of the Raman Research Institute , floated on lakes in Karnataka, tested a claimed signal of the first stars seen by the EDGES experiment in 2018 and found no evidence for it, a significant Indian result in early-universe cosmology.
Key takeaways

The universe began hot and dense 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling. Nucleosynthesis made 75 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium. The CMB is light freed at 380,000 years, now at 2.725 K. CMB ripples seeded galaxies and measure the universe's makeup. Think about it: (1) Why is the CMB so uniform yet not perfectly so? (2) What would change if the universe had formed far more helium?
Dark Energy and the Fate of the Universe
The surprise of 1998

Everyone expected gravity to slow the expansion, like a ball thrown upward. In 1998 two teams discovered the opposite: the expansion is speeding up . Something is pushing space apart. We call it dark energy , and it appears to make up about 68 percent of the universe, yet we do not know what it is.
How the discovery was made

The High-z Supernova Search Team (Brian Schmidt, Adam Riess) and the Supernova Cosmology Project (Saul Perlmutter) used distant Type Ia supernovae as standard candles. The distant ones were about 25 percent fainter than expected for a slowing universe: farther away because expansion had sped up. They shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The cosmological constant

Einstein added a term, Lambda, to his equations in 1917 to make a static universe, and dropped it after Hubble's discovery, reportedly calling it his biggest blunder. It returned as the simplest candidate for dark energy: a constant energy density of empty space, which does not dilute as space expands. The standard model of cosmology, Lambda-CDM , uses it with cold dark matter.
Why acceleration now?

Matter thins out as space grows (density falls as volume increases), but a cosmological constant stays the same. For billions of years matter dominated and the expansion slowed; around 5 to 6 billion years ago dark energy overtook matter and the expansion began to accelerate. We live at an interesting time.
The theory problem

Quantum theory suggests empty space has energy, but the predicted value is about 10^120 times too big, called the worst prediction in physics. Alternatives include quintessence (a changing field) and modified gravity. Results from the DESI survey (2024 and 2025) hinted that dark energy may weaken with time, which is intriguing but not settled.
Possible fates

Big Freeze (heat death): expansion goes on forever; galaxies fade, stars burn out in trillions of years. Favoured if dark energy is constant. Big Rip: if dark energy strengthens, it tears apart galaxies, stars, atoms. Big Crunch: if dark energy fades or reverses, the universe recollapses. Now disfavoured.
Cross-checks

The CMB shows the universe is flat, which needs more energy than matter provides. Galaxy surveys and the growth of clusters point to the same 68 percent. ESA's Euclid telescope (launched 1 July 2023) and the Vera Rubin Observatory are now measuring it better.
Mixed up ideas
'Dark energy is dark matter.' Opposite effects. 'The universe expands into a bigger space.' Nothing outside. 'We know the universe will end in a Big Freeze.' It is the best current guess.
Padmanabhan and Indian cosmologists

Thanu Padmanabhan of IUCAA (1957 to 2021) wrote widely on the cosmological constant and gravity as an emergent phenomenon. Tarun Deep Saini and others in India studied how to detect dark energy's evolution. India also contributes to Euclid and Rubin analyses, and Chandrasekhar's limit underlies why Type Ia supernovae are standard candles.
Key takeaways

Distant supernovae revealed in 1998 that expansion is accelerating. Dark energy, about 68 percent of the universe, may be Einstein's cosmological constant. The most likely fate is an eternal, cold, empty Big Freeze. Newer data, such as DESI, may test whether dark energy changes. Think about it: (1) Why did a fainter supernova mean faster expansion? (2) How would you tell a constant from a changing dark energy?
Gravitational Waves and Multi-Messenger Astronomy
A new sense for the universe

For all of history we studied the universe with light. In 2015 we heard it for the first time: ripples in space-time itself. Combined with light, neutrinos and particles, this gives astronomers several 'senses' at once, called multi-messenger astronomy.
What are gravitational waves?

Einstein's general relativity (1915) says mass bends space-time. In 1916 he predicted that accelerating masses, such as two orbiting black holes, send out ripples that travel at the speed of light. Picture a heavy ball bouncing on a trampoline: waves spread out. The ripples stretch and squeeze space as they pass.
Indirect proof first

In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a binary pulsar whose orbit shrinks exactly as fast as relativity predicts if it loses energy to gravitational waves (Nobel 1993). The waves themselves were still unseen.
LIGO and the first detection

LIGO has two L-shaped detectors with 4 km arms in Hanford and Livingston, USA. Laser light bounces along each arm; a passing wave changes the arm lengths by about 10^-21 of their size, much less than a proton's width. On 14 September 2015 , both detected GW150914 : two black holes of about 36 and 29 Suns merging 1.3 billion light-years away. It was announced in February 2016. Weiss, Barish and Thorne won the 2017 Nobel Prize. Virgo (Italy) and KAGRA (Japan) joined the network.
The neutron star merger of 2017

On 17 August 2017 , detectors heard GW170817 , two neutron stars merging. Within 1.7 seconds a gamma-ray burst was seen, then telescopes worldwide saw a glowing kilonova in the galaxy NGC 4993. It showed that gravity travels at the speed of light and that such mergers forge gold and platinum.
Many messengers

Multi-messenger astronomy combines light, gravitational waves, neutrinos and cosmic rays. SN 1987A's neutrinos arrived hours before its light. In 2017 IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the blazar TXS 0506+056 together with gamma rays. Each messenger tells a different part of the story.
Listening to the background

Pulsar timing arrays watch the ticks of millisecond pulsars. In June 2023 several teams (NANOGrav, EPTA, InPTA, PPTA) reported evidence of a low-frequency gravitational wave background, likely from supermassive black hole pairs. ESA's LISA space detector is planned for the 2030s to hear such mergers directly.
Common slips

'LIGO sees waves like a telescope.' It listens; there is no image. 'Gravitational waves are light waves.' They are ripples in space-time itself. 'They are dangerous.' By the time they reach us, they are fantastically weak.
LIGO-India and InPTA

Indian scientists (IndIGO consortium, IUCAA, RRCAT, IPR) are members of the LIGO collaboration. LIGO-India , a third LIGO detector planned at Aundha in Hingoli district, Maharashtra, received government approval in April 2023. It will sharpen sky localisation of sources. The uGMRT and the Indian Pulsar Timing Array took part in the 2023 announcement, and AstroSat's CZTI searched for X-ray counterparts of GW events.
Key takeaways

Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time from accelerating masses, predicted in 1916. LIGO detected the first on 14 September 2015 from merging black holes. GW170817 combined waves with light and proved gravity travels at c. LIGO-India and pulsar timing add Indian contributions. Think about it: (1) Why do we need several detectors around the world? (2) What could waves tell us that light cannot?
Rockets and Orbits
Getting up is the hard part

Reaching space is not about going high; it is about going sideways very fast. Everything in space travel, from satellites to Moon missions, follows from a few physics ideas: action and reaction, orbital speed and energy budgets.
How a rocket works

Newton's third law: a rocket throws exhaust backward and is pushed forward. It needs no air, so it works in vacuum. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky wrote the rocket equation in 1903: the speed gained depends on exhaust speed and on the logarithm of the mass ratio, full to empty. Because fuel must lift fuel, most of a rocket is propellant, so we use stages , dropping empty tanks. Robert Goddard flew the first liquid-fuel rocket in 1926.
Orbit is falling around

Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain: fire faster and the ball lands farther, until it falls around the curve of Earth and never lands. That is an orbit. Low Earth orbit needs about 7.8 km/s ; at about 400 km the period is about 90 minutes. Astronauts float because they and the station are in free fall.
Orbits and their uses

Low Earth orbit (200 to 2,000 km): ISS, imaging. Sun-synchronous : passes at the same local time, used for remote sensing. Geostationary : 35,786 km above the equator, period 24 hours, appears fixed in the sky, used for communication (idea by Arthur C. Clarke, 1945). Higher orbits move slower: Kepler's third law.
Escape and transfers

To leave Earth for good you need about 11.2 km/s (escape velocity). Missions rarely fly straight: a Hohmann transfer uses an elliptical path touching two orbits, the cheapest in fuel. Gravity assists let a probe steal a little of a planet's orbital energy; Voyager 2 used them to tour four planets.
Reusable rockets and the cost

Rockets used to be thrown away each time. Since the first booster landing in December 2015 (SpaceX Falcon 9), reusing boosters has cut launch costs sharply. Where space is the 'edge' is set by convention at the Karman line , 100 km up.
From V-2 to Sputnik

The German V-2 (1942) was the first rocket to reach space. After the war, Wernher von Braun and Sergei Korolev built the ones that launched the space age, from Sputnik in 1957. Orbital rules are verified every day by thousands of satellites whose paths follow Newton and Kepler.
Space myths

'There is no gravity in orbit.' Gravity is about 90 percent as strong at the ISS; it is free fall that gives weightlessness. 'Rockets push against air.' They push against their own exhaust. 'Going up is the goal.' Sideways speed is the goal.
Tipu Sultan to LVM3

Tipu Sultan's Mysore army used iron-cased rockets against the British in the 1780s and 90s, an inspiration for Congreve's rockets. ISRO's story: Vikram Sarabhai founded INCOSPAR (1962); the first sounding rocket flew from Thumba on 21 November 1963; SLV-3 put Rohini into orbit in July 1980 under A.P.J. Abdul Kalam . PSLV (first launch 1993) became a workhorse; GSLV flew with the indigenous cryogenic engine in January 2014; LVM3 launched Chandrayaan-3.
Key takeaways

Rockets work by action and reaction; staging beats the rocket equation. Orbit is free fall around Earth at about 7.8 km/s in low orbit. Geostationary orbit is 35,786 km up with a 24 hour period. Gravity assists and Hohmann transfers save fuel. Think about it: (1) Why do rockets launch eastward when they can? (2) Why does a satellite in a higher orbit move slower?
The Space Race and Apollo
A race that reached the Moon

In just 12 years, from the first satellite to the first footprints, human technology leapt from nothing to the Moon. It was driven by Cold War rivalry, and it gave us satellites, new materials, and the famous photograph of Earth from afar.
Sputnik and the shock

On 4 October 1957 the USSR launched Sputnik 1 , a 58 cm beeping sphere, the first artificial satellite. A month later Laika became the first animal in orbit. The USA launched Explorer 1 in January 1958 and founded NASA that year.
First humans in space

Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth on 12 April 1961 in Vostok 1, the first human in space. Alan Shepard followed in May as the first American. Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963; Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965.
The Moon goal

In May 1961 President Kennedy committed the USA to landing a man on the Moon before the decade ended. Gemini missions tested rendezvous and docking. The Saturn V , 110 m tall, remains the most powerful rocket flown to orbit. A tragic fire killed three Apollo 1 astronauts in January 1967.
Apollo 11 (July 1969)

On 20 July 1969 the lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Six missions landed between 1969 and 1972; twelve people walked on the Moon, and the last was Apollo 17 in December 1972. Apollo 13 (1970) suffered an explosion yet returned safely.
Why it ended, what remained

After the goal was reached, cost and attention faded. The USSR never landed. The superpowers moved to space stations (Salyut, Skylab, Mir) and cooperation, the Apollo-Soyuz link in 1975. The Outer Space Treaty (1967) bans nuclear weapons in orbit and national claims on celestial bodies.
Moon rocks and reflectors

Apollo brought back 382 kg of lunar samples, giving the Moon's age and the giant-impact clues. Mirrors left on the surface still let lasers measure the Earth-Moon distance to millimetres, showing the Moon recedes about 3.8 cm a year. Independent tracking by other nations confirmed the missions.
Settled facts

'The Moon landing was faked.' The evidence, including samples, reflectors and tracking by the USSR, is overwhelming. 'Flags wave in wind.' A rod held it out; there is no air. 'Stars missing in photos.' Exposure was set for bright sunlit ground.
Rakesh Sharma and Aryabhata

India's first satellite Aryabhata was launched by a Soviet rocket on 19 April 1975 under the Intercosmos programme. On 3 April 1984 , Squadron Leader Rakesh Sharma flew on Soyuz T-11 and spent about eight days in orbit on Salyut 7, the first Indian in space. Asked how India looked from space, he replied 'Saare jahan se achha'. India has since built its own launchers and now its own crewed programme.
Key takeaways

Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961) opened the space age. Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969; six landings, twelve walkers, ending in 1972. The Outer Space Treaty (1967) governs space activity. Rakesh Sharma (1984) was India's first astronaut. Think about it: (1) How did rivalry speed up technology? (2) Why was the Outer Space Treaty necessary?
ISRO: From Aryabhata to Chandrayaan and Aditya
A frugal space power

India began with a rocket carried on a bicycle and now lands on the Moon. ISRO is known for low-cost, application-first space work: satellites for communication, weather and farming, then planetary science.
Foundations

Vikram Sarabhai started INCOSPAR in 1962; ISRO was formed on 15 August 1969, and the Department of Space in 1972. First satellite Aryabhata (19 April 1975), then Bhaskara (1979), and SLV-3 (1980) put Rohini in orbit, making India the sixth country with orbital launch ability.
Services to the people

The INSAT series (from 1982) gave communications, television and weather forecasting. The IRS series (from 1988) images land and water for farming, forests and disasters. NavIC is India's regional navigation system, and EDUSAT served education. The PSLV (operational 1994) launched 104 satellites in one mission on 15 February 2017.
Moon missions

Chandrayaan-1 (22 October 2008) found water molecules on the Moon. Chandrayaan-2 (July 2019) orbiter works, but its Vikram lander crashed on 7 September 2019. Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023 and landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023 , making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first near the south pole. 23 August is celebrated as National Space Day. Chandrayaan-4 (a sample return mission) was approved in 2024.
Mars, Sun and eyes on the cosmos

Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 on its first try. AstroSat (28 September 2015) is India's multi-wavelength space observatory. Aditya-L1 launched 2 September 2023, reached its L1 halo orbit on 6 January 2024. XPoSat (1 January 2024) studies X-ray polarisation from black holes and neutron stars.
New frontiers

SpaDeX (launched December 2024) achieved India's first in-orbit docking in January 2025, making India the fourth country to do so. NISAR , a NASA-ISRO radar satellite, launched in 2025 to map Earth's surface changes. Gaganyaan aims to send three Indian astronauts to about 400 km for three days, with uncrewed test flights first. As of late 2026 no crewed flight had flown; the first is targeted for 2027. Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla flew to the ISS on Axiom-4 in 2025. A Bharatiya Antariksh Station is planned, with a Venus orbiter mission and an Indian on the Moon by 2040 as goals.
Success and failure

ISRO's record includes failures: PSLV's first flight (1993) failed, and Chandrayaan-2's lander crashed. Each analysis fed back: Chandrayaan-3 used a redesigned lander with a larger landing zone, and succeeded. The Pragyan rover measured surface temperature, found sulphur, and the lander detected moonquakes.
Clearing up

'Low cost means low quality.' Frugality comes from reuse of design, a skilled workforce and lower labour cost. 'Chandrayaan-3 landed at the pole.' It landed about 69 degrees south, near it, the nearest any soft landing had come. 'ISRO only builds rockets.' Most work is applications for daily life.
The policy shift

In 2020 the government opened the sector with IN-SPACe to authorise private players, and NSIL commercialises ISRO technology. Skyroot 's Vikram-S (November 2022) was India's first privately built rocket to fly, and Agnikul launched from its own private pad in 2024.
Key takeaways

ISRO began 1962 to 1969 and launched Aryabhata in 1975. Services: INSAT, IRS, NavIC; workhorse PSLV; heavy lifter LVM3. Missions: Chandrayaan-3 (2023, south pole), Mangalyaan (2014), Aditya-L1 (2023), AstroSat (2015). Next: Gaganyaan, docking, a space station, private industry. The Future: Mars, Space Stations and Beyond
The next steps off Earth

Humans have lived in orbit continuously for more than 25 years. Next come a permanent presence on the Moon, robots on icy moons and perhaps people on Mars. Several things changed: reusable rockets, private companies and new nations.
Space stations

The International Space Station , built from 1998, has had crews aboard without a break since 2 November 2000; it is planned to be retired and de-orbited around 2030 to 2031. China's Tiangong station was completed in 2022. Private commercial stations are in development. Stations teach us how bodies cope with weightlessness: bone and muscle loss, radiation and isolation.
Return to the Moon

NASA's Artemis programme plans to return crews to the lunar south pole and build a Gateway station. Artemis II, a crewed flyby of the Moon, flew in 2026; the first crewed landing is planned for later in the decade. its schedule has slipped repeatedly, so check its current status. China aims for crewed landing before 2030. Water ice in shadowed polar craters could give drinking water and rocket fuel. The Moon is also a training ground for Mars.
Mars: robots first

Perseverance (landed 2021) is caching samples, and the little helicopter Ingenuity flew 72 times (2021 to 2024). The plan to bring samples back to Earth has been delayed and under budget review. Sending people is hard: about 6 to 9 months each way, radiation, no rescue, and a thin atmosphere that makes landing tough. SpaceX's Starship , a fully reusable giant rocket, is being tested for this purpose.
Ocean worlds and beyond

ESA's JUICE (launched April 2023) and NASA's Europa Clipper (launched October 2024, arrival about 2030) will study icy moons with hidden oceans. NASA's Dragonfly will fly a drone through the air of Titan in the 2030s. Voyager 1 and 2 , launched in 1977, are now in interstellar space.
Telescopes and the next big eyes

JWST is operating; the 39 m Extremely Large Telescope in Chile and the Square Kilometre Array are being built; LISA will detect gravitational waves from space. Breakthrough Starshot proposes tiny laser-driven sails to the nearest star, but is only a concept.
What makes the future plausible

Reusable boosters have cut launch cost per kilogram severalfold. Mega-constellations (Starlink) show mass production in orbit. Meanwhile real challenges stay: radiation, closed-loop life support, space debris (over 30,000 tracked objects) and law.
Realism check

'Mars colonies soon.' Technical, medical and cost barriers are large. 'Space is empty so debris is harmless.' At 7 km/s, a bolt is a bullet. 'Space belongs to no rules.' The Outer Space Treaty (1967) and later accords govern it.
Gaganyaan to 2040

India plans Gaganyaan (crewed low-orbit flights), the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (first module planned around 2028, full station by 2035), Chandrayaan-4 sample return, a Venus Orbiter Mission (about 2028), and a crewed Moon landing by 2040. Private launchers such as Skyroot and Agnikul are building small rockets. Timelines for such missions often shift.
Key takeaways

Space stations keep humans in orbit; ISS retires around 2030. Artemis and Chinese plans aim for the Moon; Mars sample return and crewed missions are far harder. Icy-moon missions search for life. India's plans: Gaganyaan, its own station by 2035, Moon landing by 2040. Think about it: (1) Why is the Moon a stepping stone to Mars? (2) How should humanity handle space debris?
